clinicalPearls: A myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by a persistently raised platelet count from clonal megakaryocyte proliferation
Driver mutations are found in JAK2, CALR or MPL, with a minority triple-negative
Many patients are asymptomatic; others have vasomotor symptoms such as headache, erythromelalgia and visual disturbance
Both thrombosis and, at very high platelet counts, bleeding (from acquired von Willebrand syndrome) can occur
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring reactive thrombocytosis and other myeloproliferative neoplasms to be ruled out
Risk-adapted management uses aspirin and, in higher-risk patients, platelet-lowering cytoreduction
reference.pathophysiology: Essential thrombocythaemia is a clonal stem cell disorder in which mutations in JAK2, CALR or MPL activate thrombopoietin-receptor signalling, driving excess megakaryopoiesis and a sustained rise in platelets. The qualitatively abnormal platelets, together with the raised count and interactions with the vessel wall, increase thrombotic risk. Paradoxically, extreme thrombocytosis can cause bleeding through an acquired von Willebrand syndrome, as large von Willebrand multimers are adsorbed and degraded. Long-term clonal evolution can lead to myelofibrosis or, less often, acute leukaemia.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film
JAK2, CALR and MPL mutation analysis
Bone marrow examination assessing megakaryocyte morphology
Exclusion of reactive causes (inflammation, iron deficiency, bleeding)
von Willebrand assessment at very high platelet counts
redFlags: Bleeding with extreme thrombocytosis (acquired von Willebrand syndrome)
Progressive splenomegaly or cytopenias suggesting fibrotic transformation
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is near-normal for many patients with appropriate risk management, though thrombosis and haemorrhage cause morbidity and a minority transform to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia.
pitfalls: Treating reactive thrombocytosis as essential thrombocythaemia
Giving aspirin at extreme counts without checking for acquired von Willebrand syndrome
Missing prefibrotic myelofibrosis on marrow morphology
management: Low-dose aspirin to control microvascular and vasomotor symptoms and reduce thrombosis, once acquired von Willebrand syndrome has been excluded
Risk-adapted cytoreduction in higher-risk disease, with hydroxycarbamide first-line and interferon-alfa (preferred in younger patients and pregnancy) or anagrelide as alternatives
Optimise cardiovascular risk factors given the thrombotic tendency
At extreme thrombocytosis with bleeding, withhold antiplatelet therapy and manage the acquired von Willebrand syndrome
Monitor the platelet count and full blood count, watching for transformation to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia
